proficiency_levels.description: Notices obvious signs of client discomfort and adjusts — softening tone or pausing — but may inadvertently create pressure through over-probing. Begins to understand that safety requires action, not just good intentions. Can create safety in one-on-one conversations but struggles in group settings.
coaching_questions: Can you describe a time you sensed a client was uncomfortable — what were the signs, and how did you respond?
What is the difference between being polite and creating genuine psychological safety?
How do you create safety in a group setting compared to one-on-one?

proficiency_levels.description: Deliberately creates safety through specific practices — setting expectations about confidentiality, naming difficult dynamics, and modelling vulnerability. Recognises when a client is performing confidence rather than feeling it and adjusts the approach. Maintains psychological safety even when delivering challenging messages.
coaching_questions: Walk me through the specific practices you use to create safety — norm-setting, confidentiality framing, modelling vulnerability.
How do you recognise when a client is performing confidence rather than feeling it?
How do you maintain psychological safety even when delivering difficult or unwelcome messages?

proficiency_levels.description: Intuitively calibrates how much challenge a client can absorb and paces the conversation accordingly. Creates conditions where clients voluntarily share information they initially intended to withhold. Manages the emotional temperature of multi-stakeholder meetings so that everyone feels safe enough to contribute honestly.
coaching_questions: Tell me about a time a client voluntarily shared something they initially intended to withhold — what created the conditions for that?
How do you calibrate how much challenge a client can absorb and pace the conversation accordingly?
When have you managed the emotional temperature of a multi-stakeholder meeting so that everyone felt safe to contribute honestly?

proficiency_levels.description: Has a presence that makes psychological safety the default — clients relax and open up without any visible technique being applied. Creates safety at the organisational level, enabling honest conversations that were previously impossible. Others experience the relationship itself as transformative, independent of the consulting content.
coaching_questions: Describe a relationship where your presence made safety the default — without any visible technique being applied.
How have you created safety at the organisational level, enabling conversations that were previously impossible?
When has the client experienced the relationship itself as transformative, independent of the consulting content?

building_blocks.description:
Use questions not primarily to gather information but to expand the client's thinking, challenge assumptions, and open new perspectives. 
Process what is said, how it is said, and what is withheld to arrive at a full picture of the client's experience.
building_blocks.consulting_example: SPIN questioning framework (Situation, Problem, Implication, Need-payoff)

proficiency_levels.description: Asks questions primarily to fill a checklist or data template rather than to explore the client's thinking. Listens for answers to their own questions rather than for what the client is actually communicating. Misses nonverbal cues and does not notice when something important is being left unsaid.
coaching_questions: What was the purpose of the questions you asked in the last client meeting — what were you trying to learn?
Can you paraphrase what the client told you and what you think they meant by it?
Did you notice any nonverbal cues during the conversation? What did they tell you?

proficiency_levels.description: Asks follow-up questions that show genuine curiosity and can paraphrase what the client said to confirm understanding. Begins to notice tone, hesitation, and body language as sources of information. Listens more fully in one-on-one settings but may revert to checklist mode in group interviews.
coaching_questions: When you followed up on an answer, what prompted you to dig deeper?
Can you describe what you heard in the client's tone or hesitation, beyond just the words?
How does your questioning approach differ in a one-on-one interview versus a group setting?

proficiency_levels.description: Uses questions strategically — to expand thinking, challenge assumptions, or open new perspectives rather than just to gather data. Processes what is said, how it is said, and what is withheld to arrive at a full picture. Holds silence comfortably, allowing the client space to arrive at deeper reflections.
coaching_questions: Walk me through how you used questions strategically in this conversation — to expand thinking, challenge assumptions, or open new perspectives.
What did you learn from what the client did not say, and how did you process that?
When did you hold silence and let the client arrive at a deeper reflection? What happened?

proficiency_levels.description: Asks questions that the client has never been asked before, unlocking new self-awareness or strategic insight. Hears the system behind the individual — detecting organisational patterns, political undercurrents, and cultural norms from a single conversation. Intuitively knows when to probe and when to let a topic rest.
coaching_questions: Tell me about a question you asked that the client had never been asked before — what did it unlock?
How do you hear the system behind the individual — detecting organisational patterns or political undercurrents from a single conversation?
When have you intuitively known when to probe further and when to let a topic rest?

proficiency_levels.description: Questions function as interventions — each one shifts the client's thinking in a way that is itself valuable, independent of the answer. Listens at a level that makes the client feel more deeply understood than in any other professional relationship. The questioning and listening practice becomes a model that clients adopt in their own leadership.
coaching_questions: Describe a question that functioned as an intervention — where the question itself shifted the client's thinking, independent of the answer.
When has a client felt more deeply understood in conversation with you than in any other professional relationship?
How has your questioning practice become a model that the client has adopted in their own leadership?

building_blocks.description: Distinguishing presenting requests from underlying needs, and surface symptoms from systemic causes, before any advice or action is offered.
building_blocks.consulting_example: Presenting problem vs. root cause analysis

proficiency_levels.description: Takes the client's stated request at face value without exploring whether it addresses the real need. Does not distinguish between what the client asks for and what the client actually needs. May deliver exactly what was requested while missing the opportunity to solve the real problem.
coaching_questions: Is the work you are doing addressing what the client asked for, what they need, or both?
How did you validate that the stated request matches the underlying problem?
Has the client's real need differed from their initial request? How did you discover that?

proficiency_levels.description: Begins to notice gaps between the stated request and the underlying situation, especially when the evidence does not fit the brief. Asks clarifying questions that occasionally surface a deeper need but does not yet do this systematically. Recognises that clients may not fully understand their own needs but is unsure how to navigate that without seeming presumptuous.
coaching_questions: Can you give me an example of a gap you noticed between what a client asked for and what they actually needed?
How do you explore whether a presenting request masks a deeper issue without seeming presumptuous?
When have your clarifying questions surfaced a need the client had not articulated?

proficiency_levels.description: Systematically explores the gap between the presenting request and the underlying need before proposing any solution. Surfaces symptoms versus systemic causes through structured inquiry and gentle challenge. Reframes the engagement scope when the original brief does not match the real problem, gaining client buy-in for the shift.
coaching_questions: Walk me through how you systematically explored the gap between the stated request and the underlying need.
How did you distinguish symptoms from systemic causes before proposing a solution?
When you needed to reframe the engagement scope, how did you gain client buy-in for the shift?

proficiency_levels.description: Senses the real need early — often within the first conversation — and navigates toward it without dismissing the client's stated request. Holds multiple hypotheses about what the client truly needs and refines them as the relationship deepens. Reframes needs in ways that the client experiences as illuminating rather than threatening.
coaching_questions: Tell me about a time you sensed the real need within the first conversation — what gave it away?
How do you hold multiple hypotheses about what the client truly needs and refine them over time?
When have you reframed a client's need in a way they experienced as illuminating rather than threatening?

proficiency_levels.description: Sees the client's need within the full context of their organisational, competitive, and personal situation simultaneously. Helps the client discover their own real need rather than simply diagnosing it for them. The need-framing process itself builds capability in the client, making them better at defining their own challenges going forward.
coaching_questions: Describe how you helped a client discover their own real need rather than simply diagnosing it for them.
How do you see the client's need within the full context of their organisational, competitive, and personal situation?
When has your need-framing process built capability in the client — making them better at defining their own challenges?

building_blocks.description: Actively manage the dimensions of trustworthiness — expertise, reliability, benevolence, integrity — across the full arc of a relationship, not just at its start.

proficiency_levels.description: Focuses on demonstrating competence without attending to reliability, benevolence, or integrity. Builds rapport superficially — small talk and friendliness — without creating deeper professional trust. Does not recognise that trust is actively earned and can be actively eroded.
coaching_questions: How do you demonstrate competence to a new client?
What do you do when you cannot deliver on a commitment?
How do you build rapport beyond surface-level small talk?

proficiency_levels.description: Follows through on commitments consistently and begins to earn a reputation for reliability. Recognises when trust has been damaged and feels the impact but does not yet know how to repair it. Builds trust within the immediate project team but has not yet extended it to senior client stakeholders.
coaching_questions: Can you give me an example of a commitment you followed through on that strengthened a client's trust?
When has trust been damaged in a client relationship? What happened and what did you do?
How do you build trust with senior stakeholders you do not interact with day to day?

proficiency_levels.description: Actively manages all four dimensions of trust — expertise, reliability, benevolence, and integrity — through deliberate behaviours. Keeps self-orientation low by genuinely prioritising the client's interest over personal or firm interests. Addresses trust breaches directly and promptly, taking responsibility and changing behaviour.
coaching_questions: Walk me through how you actively manage credibility, reliability, benevolence, and integrity in a client relationship.
How do you keep self-orientation low — genuinely prioritising the client's interest over your own?
Describe a trust breach you addressed directly — how did you take responsibility and change behaviour?

proficiency_levels.description: Has earned deep trust that extends beyond the current engagement — the client consults them on issues outside the project scope. Intuitively knows which dimension of trust needs attention at any given moment and acts accordingly. Manages trust across multiple relationships simultaneously, calibrating differently for each stakeholder.
coaching_questions: Tell me about a time a client consulted you on an issue outside the project scope — what had you done to earn that level of trust?
How do you manage trust across multiple stakeholders simultaneously, calibrating differently for each?
When have you intuitively sensed which dimension of trust needed attention and acted on it?

proficiency_levels.description: Trust is so deeply established that it becomes a strategic asset — enabling conversations, decisions, and changes that would be impossible without it. Models trustworthiness so consistently that it sets the relational standard for the entire engagement team. The trust built outlasts the consulting relationship and becomes part of the client's professional network.
coaching_questions: Describe how the trust you have built has enabled conversations, decisions, or changes that would have been impossible without it.
How has your modelling of trustworthiness set the relational standard for the entire engagement team?
When has the trust you built outlasted the consulting relationship and become part of the client's professional network?

building_blocks.description: Calibrating guidance to genuine uncertainty, explaining reasoning transparently, and framing recommendations as options rather than verdicts.

proficiency_levels.description: Defaults to giving direct advice based on the analysis, without considering the leader's context, constraints, or readiness. Presents recommendations as the correct answer rather than as one of several options. Does not recognise that coaching a senior leader requires a fundamentally different posture than delivering a recommendation.
coaching_questions: How do you typically present a recommendation to a senior leader?
Do you frame your advice as the right answer or as one of several options? Why?
What do you do when a senior leader disagrees with your recommendation?

proficiency_levels.description: Recognises that senior leaders need to feel ownership of the solution and begins to frame recommendations as options. Can explain reasoning when asked but does not yet proactively offer transparency about assumptions and trade-offs. Adjusts tone for seniority but does not yet calibrate to the individual leader's decision-making style.
coaching_questions: How do you adjust your tone and approach when speaking with a C-suite leader versus a mid-level manager?
Can you describe a time you explained your reasoning transparently — including what you were unsure about?
When you framed a recommendation as options, how did the leader respond compared to when you gave a single answer?

proficiency_levels.description: Frames recommendations as options with explicit trade-offs, allowing the leader to exercise genuine choice. Explains reasoning transparently, including what is known, what is uncertain, and what was assumed. Calibrates guidance to the leader's genuine uncertainty — providing structure where they lack clarity and space where they need to think.
coaching_questions: Walk me through how you framed the trade-offs in your last recommendation to a senior leader.
How do you calibrate guidance to the leader's genuine uncertainty — providing structure where they lack clarity and space where they need to think?
How transparent are you about your assumptions and what is unknown?

proficiency_levels.description: Reads the leader's emotional and cognitive state and adjusts the coaching approach in real time. Knows when to provide frameworks and when to simply hold space for the leader to think aloud. Challenges the leader's thinking respectfully but directly, in ways that expand rather than narrow their perspective.
coaching_questions: Tell me about a time you challenged a senior leader's thinking respectfully but directly — what was the effect?
How do you read a leader's emotional and cognitive state and adjust your coaching approach in real time?
When have you known when to provide a framework versus when to simply hold space for the leader to think aloud?

proficiency_levels.description: Functions as a true thought partner — the leader seeks them out not for answers but for the quality of the thinking process. Helps leaders see their own blind spots without creating defensiveness or dependence. The coaching relationship enables the leader to make better decisions long after the engagement ends.
coaching_questions: Describe a relationship where a senior leader sought you out not for answers but for the quality of the thinking process.
How do you help leaders see their own blind spots without creating defensiveness or dependence?
When has a coaching relationship enabled a leader to make better decisions long after the engagement ended?

building_blocks.description: Holding the client's individual situation and their organisational, cultural, and relational ecosystem simultaneously in view when diagnosing and advising.

proficiency_levels.description: Analyses the client's problem in isolation from their broader organisational, cultural, or competitive context. Applies the same diagnostic lens regardless of industry, culture, or political dynamics. May produce technically sound advice that fails because it ignores contextual realities.
coaching_questions: What do you know about this client's organisational culture, and how did you learn it?
How did you factor in the client's political dynamics when developing your recommendation?
Could this recommendation fail for reasons unrelated to its analytical quality?

proficiency_levels.description: Recognises that context matters and asks basic questions about organisational structure, culture, and stakeholder dynamics. Can incorporate contextual information when it is provided but does not yet proactively seek it. May over-index on one contextual dimension (e.g., politics) while neglecting others (e.g., culture).
coaching_questions: What contextual questions do you typically ask at the start of an engagement?
Can you identify which contextual factors — culture, politics, capability — you paid the most attention to and which you may have overlooked?
When has a recommendation you supported failed because of contextual factors? What did you learn?

proficiency_levels.description: Systematically maps the client's organisational, cultural, and relational ecosystem before diagnosing or advising. Holds the individual problem and the broader context simultaneously in view, adjusting recommendations accordingly. Identifies when a technically correct recommendation will fail due to cultural, political, or capability constraints.
coaching_questions: Walk me through how you mapped this client's organisational, cultural, and relational ecosystem before advising.
How do you hold the individual problem and the broader context simultaneously when developing recommendations?
When did you identify that a technically correct recommendation would fail due to cultural or political constraints?

proficiency_levels.description: Reads organisational context rapidly and accurately, often grasping the real power dynamics and cultural norms faster than the client expects. Integrates context so seamlessly that recommendations feel native to the organisation rather than externally imposed. Anticipates how context will evolve as the engagement progresses and adjusts framing proactively.
coaching_questions: Tell me about a time you grasped the real power dynamics and cultural norms of an organisation faster than the client expected.
How do you integrate context so seamlessly that your recommendations feel native to the organisation?
When have you anticipated how the context would evolve during the engagement and adjusted your framing proactively?

proficiency_levels.description: Sees the full system — competitive, regulatory, cultural, interpersonal, historical — as a single, integrated picture. Uses contextual insight as a strategic tool, reframing the client's situation in ways that reveal opportunities invisible from inside the organisation. The contextual framing itself becomes one of the most valued contributions of the engagement.
coaching_questions: Describe a situation where your contextual insight revealed an opportunity that was invisible from inside the organisation.
How do you see the full system — competitive, regulatory, cultural, interpersonal, historical — as a single, integrated picture?
When has your contextual framing been one of the most valued contributions of the engagement?

building_blocks.description:
Build and sustain a client network.
Proactively cultivate relationships beyond active engagements to generate trust, referrals, and future opportunities.

proficiency_levels.description: Interacts only with clients on active engagements and does not maintain relationships between projects. Views networking as a transactional activity — reaching out only when something is needed. Does not yet see relationship-building as a professional skill that requires deliberate practice.
coaching_questions: How many former clients or professional contacts have you stayed in touch with after a project ended?
What does your typical approach to maintaining professional relationships look like?
Do you think of networking as something you do deliberately or something that happens naturally?

proficiency_levels.description: Maintains contact with a small number of former clients through occasional check-ins. Attends industry events but struggles to convert introductions into meaningful professional relationships. Recognises the value of a network but builds it reactively rather than strategically.
coaching_questions: How do you stay relevant to a former client between engagements?
Can you describe a professional event where you successfully turned an introduction into a meaningful relationship?
Do you have a networking strategy, or do you build relationships reactively?

proficiency_levels.description: Proactively cultivates relationships beyond active engagements, staying visible and relevant to former clients and industry contacts. Develops a deliberate networking strategy — targeting specific relationships, industries, or roles — aligned with personal and firm development goals. Provides value to contacts without expecting immediate return, building goodwill and trust.
coaching_questions: Walk me through your networking strategy — which relationships are you targeting and why?
How do you provide value to contacts without expecting immediate return?
How is your networking strategy aligned with your personal development goals and the firm's priorities?

proficiency_levels.description: Maintains a broad, active network that generates referrals, insights, and opportunities with minimal explicit effort. Intuitively knows which relationships to invest in and when to re-engage a dormant connection. Serves as a connector — introducing people across their network in ways that create mutual value.
coaching_questions: Tell me about a relationship you re-engaged after a long dormant period — how did you know it was the right time?
How do you serve as a connector — introducing people across your network to create mutual value?
When has a relationship in your network generated a referral or opportunity without you explicitly asking?

proficiency_levels.description: Has built a network that functions as a strategic asset for the firm, not just for personal business development. Relationships are so deep and multidimensional that the consultant is seen as a permanent part of the client's extended professional circle. Network effects compound — each relationship strengthens the others, creating an ecosystem of trust and opportunity.
coaching_questions: Describe how your network has become a strategic asset for the firm, not just for your personal business development.
When have network effects compounded — where each relationship strengthened the others?
How do you sustain relationships so deep that you are seen as a permanent part of the client's professional circle?

building_blocks.description:
Consistently deliver insights, connections, or perspective that exceed the stated scope of work.
Leave the client better off in ways they did not initially ask for, reinforcing the relationship and the firm's reputation.

proficiency_levels.description: Delivers exactly what was scoped without looking for opportunities to exceed expectations. Does not recognise moments where a small additional insight, connection, or effort could significantly increase the client's perceived value. Views the engagement scope as a ceiling rather than a floor.
coaching_questions: Have you identified any opportunities to help the client beyond the stated scope of work?
What would exceeding expectations look like on this engagement?
How do you distinguish between adding value and scope creep?

proficiency_levels.description: Occasionally identifies an opportunity to add value beyond the scope but hesitates to share it without being asked. Shares relevant articles or ideas ad hoc but does not yet make it a consistent practice. Begins to understand that perceived value is shaped by more than just deliverable quality.
coaching_questions: Can you describe a time you spotted an opportunity to add value but hesitated to raise it? What held you back?
How consistently do you share relevant articles, ideas, or connections with clients?
What shapes a client's perception of value beyond the quality of the deliverable itself?

proficiency_levels.description: Consistently identifies and shares insights, connections, or perspectives that exceed the stated scope without overstepping. Positions value-adds so they feel generous rather than like scope creep or upselling. Tracks client needs and interests beyond the project, proactively surfacing relevant information from other engagements or industries.
coaching_questions: Walk me through the unsolicited insights or connections you have provided to this client — how did you identify them?
How do you position value-adds so they feel generous rather than like scope creep or upselling?
How do you track client needs and interests beyond the project scope?

proficiency_levels.description: Creates a pattern of unexpected value that becomes a defining feature of the client relationship. Intuitively identifies the two or three things the client does not know they need and delivers them at exactly the right moment. Adds value in ways that strengthen the client's internal standing — making them look good to their own stakeholders.
coaching_questions: Tell me about a value-add you delivered at exactly the right moment — how did you know the timing was right?
How do you add value in ways that strengthen the client's internal standing — making them look good to their own stakeholders?
When has your pattern of unexpected value become a defining feature of the client relationship?

proficiency_levels.description: Has redefined what the client expects from a consulting relationship through the consistent quality and relevance of unsolicited contributions. Value creation extends beyond the engagement — the consultant's insights, frameworks, and connections continue to benefit the client long after the project ends. The client views the relationship itself as one of the most valuable assets in their professional life.
coaching_questions: Describe how you have redefined what a client expects from a consulting relationship through your unsolicited contributions.
When have your insights, frameworks, or connections continued to benefit the client long after the project ended?
When has the client viewed the relationship itself as one of the most valuable assets in their professional life?
